subject: future
topic: Machines can now guess what you are looking at from brain scans
angle: Generative models can reconstruct natural images, semantic details, and even subjective experiences like dreams or illusions from fMRI brain activity.
title: Decoding the Private Mind

hooks.text: Can a machine see your dreams?
You think your dreams are private. Machines can decode them.
Your internal imagery is becoming a data point.
A flickering image in your mind before sleep.

reveal.headline: Machines can reconstruct your dreams from brain activity.
reveal.body: Generative models can identify links between functional magnetic resonance imaging patterns and verbal reports of visual imagery during sleep.

explain.headline: Neural networks decode your internal visuals.
explain.body: Deep neural networks and diffusion models can translate fMRI signals into images. They reconstruct low-level layouts, semantic details, and even illusory percepts.

matters.headline: Your internal world is becoming data.
matters.body: That may be why the line between your private thoughts and machine-readable data is thinning. Your subjective experiences are becoming accessible to decoding.

example.headline: A quiet moment before sleep.
example.body: You lie in bed and see a fleeting image of a forest or a house. The machine sees the patterns your brain makes to create that image.

question.headline: What part of your mind remains private?

stat.label: distance for reconstructing semantic details of original images from fMRI patterns

claims.text: Machine-learning models can predict the contents of visual imagery during the sleep-onset period by discovering links between human functional magnetic resonance imaging patterns and verbal reports.
claims.quote: Here we present a neural decoding approach in which machine-learning models predict the contents of visual imagery during the sleep-onset period, given measured brain activity, by discovering links between human functional magnetic resonance imaging patterns and verbal reports

claims.text: A brain decoding technique combined with deep neural network representations can reconstruct illusory percepts as images from brain activity.
claims.quote: Here, we leverage a brain decoding technique combined with deep neural network (DNN) representations to reconstruct illusory percepts as images from brain activity.

claims.text: The DBDM model achieved Inception, CLIP and SwAV distances of 0.611, 0.225 and 0.405, respectively, when reconstructing semantic details of original images from fMRI patterns.
claims.quote: In particular, the best performance is achieved by DBDM in reconstructing the semantic details of the original image; the Inception, CLIP and SwAV distances are 0. 611, 0. 225 and 0. 405, respectively.

claims.text: A two-stage framework called Brain-Diffuser can reconstruct images that capture low-level properties and overall layout from fMRI signals.
claims.quote: In the first stage, starting from fMRI signals, we reconstruct images that capture low-level properties and overall layout using a VDVAE (Very Deep Variational Autoencoder) model.

claims.text: The NeuralDiffuser model provides detailed cues in the form of gradients to achieve both semantic coherence and detail fidelity when reconstructing visual stimuli.
claims.quote: This extension of the bottom-up process for diffusion models achieves both semantic coherence and detail fidelity when reconstructing visual stimuli.

verdict: Multiple studies demonstrate that diffusion models and deep neural networks can successfully decode fMRI signals into visual reconstructions ranging from low-level layouts to complex semantic details.
caveat: The research focuses on reconstructing visual stimuli and experiences rather than real-time, high-fidelity visual streaming.
caption:
Machines are beginning to bridge the gap between human thought and digital reconstruction.

Studies show that diffusion models can decode fMRI signals to recreate visual layouts and semantic details. This research does not yet allow for real-time, high-fidelity visual streaming.

How does it feel to know your internal imagery is becoming decodable?
